content_metadata.description: This video introduces and explains the concept of naming ionic compounds with polyatomic ions, including sulfate and phosphate, and demonstrates the use of the crossover method for balancing charges in chemical formulas.

qAndA.question: What is the name of the polyatomic ion SO4 2-?
What is the chemical formula for calcium phosphate?

qAndA.answer: Parentheses indicate that there are two phosphate groups (PO4) in the compound.
qAndA.question: Why is it important to use parentheses in the formula for calcium phosphate?

qAndA.answer: Zero, as the positive and negative charges balance each other out.
qAndA.question: What is the overall charge of an ionic compound?

qAndA.answer: The crossover method, where the numerical value of each ion's charge becomes the subscript of the other ion.
qAndA.question: What visual method is used to determine the subscripts in the formula of an ionic compound?

text_to_speech: Hi, there my name is Dr. Scott Melideo, and in this short under 5-minute video, we will go over ionic compounds have a polyatomic ion in them. The assumptions I am making in this video are that you already know how to determine the name and formula of a binary ionic compound and the names and formulas for the polyatomic ions being talked about, which are sulfate, SO42- and phosphate, PO43-. 1st we will go from the formula to the name. When naming an ionic compound that has a polyatomic ion the same rules apply as if you were naming a binary ionic compound, with the only exception being you do not change the name of the polyatomic ion if it is an anion. Let’s look at the formula Na2SO4, what would the name be? Pause the video to give yourself some time. Did you say sodium sulfate? Yes? Great! If not did you remember that sulfate’s name does not change? Next, let’s going the other direction and look at the compound named calcium phosphate. Pause the video to give yourself some time. Did you write the following, Ca3(PO4)2? If not remember, that the calcium ion is +2, and phosphate is -3. Also, you need the parentheses to show how many phosphates you have without them this is what it would look like- Ca3PO42. Which as you can see is pretty different. We can use either the crossover method or the formula to check our work. As shown. Thank you for watching this video! If you watched all the videos related to ionic compounds thank you for spending time.
